metadata.file_name: 2. Zhu et al. (2025). Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models.pdf
metadata.title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study analyzed PISA 2022 mathematics performance for the United States, merging student and school files using the school ID (CNTSCHID) so that school-level predictors were assigned to students within the same school. The analytic sample comprised 4,552 students in 154 schools, with grade information reported (primarily 10th grade). Although the authors followed PISA user guidance for computing estimates for each plausible value, they explicitly did not include sampling weights in the ML analyses, arguing that weighting might be less critical for ML model configuration and citing evidence that ML can still produce reliable results under complex multistage clustered designs. The paper therefore treats the ML training/testing as effectively unweighted with respect to PISA sampling weights, while still using the official PV framework for the outcome.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 microdata for 15-year-old students in the United States. Merged student and school questionnaires using CNTSCHID so that school-level predictors were attached to students in the same school. The analytic dataset was then reduced via preprocessing: removed predictors with >50% missing values; removed identical predictors (same values for all students); removed redundant predictors (e.g., retained ESCS and excluded the component DVs used to compute it); and imputed remaining missing predictor values using missForest (RF-based imputation). The final modeling dataset was split into training (80%, N=3644) and test (20%, N=908), and models were trained separately for each of the 10 PVs (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) with results averaged.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison using reduced predictor sets: Random Forest (selected 5 predictors) rMSE full=63.69 vs reduced=69.82; training time full=1098.72 vs reduced=129.27. XGBoost (selected 10 predictors) rMSE full=60.47 vs reduced=66.39; training time full=8.23 vs reduced=4.14. LightGBM (selected 10 predictors) rMSE full=60.43 vs reduced=66.36; training time full=44.28 vs reduced=22.93. Best model by accuracy+efficiency: XGBoost with reduced-model rMSE=66.39 and ARE≈9.79%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for U.S. students, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-learning to predict mathematics achievement (across PV1MATH–PV10MATH), finding that all three ensemble tree models achieved high accuracy with substantially reduced predictor sets and that XGBoost performed best (lowest reduced-model rMSE among the compared models and fastest training time). This indicates that focusing instructional and support efforts on a small set of high-yield factors—especially self-efficacy and foundational math familiarity—may be a more efficient strategy for improving math outcomes, though the study is predictive (not causal) and does not incorporate PISA sampling weights in the ML training.

data.outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2022 mathematics plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) for U.S. 15-year-olds (N=4,552 in 154 schools) and trained three ensemble tree-based ML models—Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM—to predict mathematics achievement. After cleaning predictors (dropping >50% missing predictors, removing identical/redundant variables) and imputing remaining missing values with missForest, the authors split data into training (80%) and test (20%) and performed five-fold cross-validation within training. For each PV, they fitted each model with all predictors, then used forward selection with an absolute relative error (ARE) criterion of 0.1 to obtain reduced predictor sets; results were averaged across the 10 PVs. Reduced-model performance showed high accuracy for all models, with XGBoost identified as best by both accuracy and efficiency (reduced-model rMSE=66.39; training time=4.14s), slightly outperforming LightGBM (rMSE=66.36; 22.93s) and RF (rMSE=69.82; 129.27s). The study uses ALE plots for interpretation and does not apply sampling weights in ML, so findings should be treated as associations rather than causal effects.
